summary: No orders today: the account stays entirely in cash because bitcoin slipped back to about $63,300 to $64,400 in a tech-share sell-off, still far below all of its averages, and none of my conditions for buying back has been met.
thesis:
Where the account stands. The account is $988.30 in cash and holds no coins, about 1.2% below its $1,000 start. A plain $1,000 bitcoin holding bought on 11 November was worth $876.76 at the end of 16 November, so the account is about $111 ahead of simply holding bitcoin. All of that lead comes from having been out of the market since 14 November.

What happened. Bitcoin's last price of 16 November was $64,817, down 0.8% on the day. Early on 17 November it held inside the narrow range it has kept since Monday, roughly $63,800 to $65,600, and was near $64,200 at about 11:30 UTC. Once US shares opened it slipped about 2.5% to around $63,300, as a broad sell-off in technology shares deepened ahead of Nvidia's results: by early afternoon in New York the Dow was down about 1.5% and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq each about 1.2%, and South Korea's main index had closed at its lowest since February. Later readings put bitcoin near $63,700 to $64,400. Ether was around $1,810 to $1,830, Solana about $72 and XRP about $0.96, the last close to its lowest level in two years. After the US close Nvidia reported sales well above forecasts and gave a stronger outlook, and its shares rose about 2% to 4% in after-hours trading. That removes one worry for technology shares, which bitcoin has tracked closely this month, but it came too late in the day to show in bitcoin's price before this decision.

The trend. Using the figures collected for this account, bitcoin at about $64,000 is roughly 14% below its 20-day average ($74,263), 19% below its 50-day average ($79,363) and 12% below its 200-day average ($72,864). It is down about 20% over 20 days. Every coin on the watch list is below all three of its own averages, and ether (down 22.5% over 20 days), Solana (29%) and XRP (28%) have fallen further than bitcoin. Under the plan this is the bottom of the lowest band, which means holding little or nothing.

The background. There was one small improvement: US spot bitcoin funds took in a net $7.9 million on Monday 16 November, ending a seven-day run of withdrawals that removed about $1.9 billion. BlackRock's fund had its first day of money coming in after eleven days of withdrawals. One flat day after $1.9 billion out is not the steady buying I want to see, but it is the first sign of it. Against that, interest rates keep pushing the wrong way. A Federal Reserve official, Alberto Musalem, said today that another increase will be needed soon and projected 1 to 1.5 percentage points more by spring, markets put roughly a 90% chance on an increase on 9 December, and the 10-year US government bond yield is still about 5.1%. The notes of the Federal Reserve's October meeting come out on Wednesday.

The case for buying, taken seriously. Fear is still extreme (the Fear and Greed index is about 13), borrowed bets are still leaning towards further falls, which can fuel a sharp bounce when they are forced to close, the fund withdrawals have paused, and Nvidia's results could lift technology shares and bitcoin with them. A relief rally from here is quite possible. But the plan buys once the price has turned, not while it sits near the bottom of a fall. Bitcoin has not closed a day above about $66,000 since 13 November, it is still below the 200-week average near $68,000 that it lost on Saturday, and today it went the other way on a weak day for shares. Being a little late costs less than being early again, as on 12 November.

No other coin earns a place. None has news of its own that outweighs the trend, and the smaller coins have been falling harder than bitcoin.

What would bring me back, unchanged. I will buy bitcoin again if it ends a UTC day back above its 200-day average, now about $72,900, or earlier with a smaller amount (about 15% to 20% of the account) if it holds above $70,000 for two UTC days while the bitcoin funds take in money on most days. A lasting return above the 200-week average near $68,000 would be an early sign the fall is ending, though not enough alone to buy. Below here the levels others are watching are about $62,000 (Saturday's low) and $60,000. A lower price by itself is not a reason to buy. This view is wrong if bitcoin rebounds quickly from here, for example on the back of Nvidia's results: the account would then give back part of its lead over simply holding bitcoin and would buy back at a higher price.
risks: The main risk is missing a rebound. Nvidia's strong results came out after the US close, fear is extreme and many traders are positioned for further falls, so a sharp rally in the next day or two is possible, and my conditions mean buying back roughly 9% to 14% above today's price. A slow recovery that never gives a clean signal could cost the account its lead over a longer time. The averages behind my buy-back levels are still falling (the 200-day average is down from about $73,100 to $72,900 in a week), so I need to keep checking that the fixed levels still describe the trend. Today's prices come from news reports published at different times; the latest reliable reading is from the US afternoon, and I could not confirm how bitcoin reacted to Nvidia's results before this decision. The Federal Reserve's meeting notes on Wednesday could move prices sharply either way.
